title: APE1 binds and processes abasic sites present in i-motif DNA and cooperates with PCBP1 in maintenance of telomeric stability.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Listed the whole Open Science Framework (OSF, a public file-sharing site for research) project dv24s through its interface: 5 folders, no tables. Downloaded and unzipped 'Raw data CD.zip' (36 KB) - it holds 11 JASCO spectrometer binary files (.jws) naming exactly 5 DNA samples (C-NAT, AP14, AP16, AP17, AP20) plus a buffer blank; opened one and read its header (instrument J-715, sample 'crichAp14_6uM_360_220_10'). Also unzipped the journal supplement (8.9 MB): the only file is a 24 MB Word document with 35 text paragraphs, 0 tables, i.e. methods and figure legends only.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Binding constants and cleavage percentages exist only as bar charts and fitted numbers inside figures (text says 'K D values, expressed in nM, are reported (n = 3)'); I never saw them as a column. The paper's statement that raw single-molecule imaging data needs approval from the corresponding author was read, not tested.

a1_downloadable.note: The OSF project is public and I downloaded a file from it with no login. Partial caveat: single-molecule imaging raw data is held back behind an approval request to the author.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL, verified in the files. Nothing anywhere is a feature/label table. The deposited files are proprietary instrument binaries: JASCO .jws spectra, GraphPad .pzfx plots, Bio-Rad .zpcr quantitative PCR runs, LI-COR blot images, Leica .lif microscopy stacks. Any label (percent cleaved, binding constant) would have to be re-derived from gel images or digitised off published bar charts.

a3_inputs_present.note: The DNA sequences used are written out in the methods text, so inputs could be typed in by hand - but there are only a handful of them.

a4_units_stated.note: Units are stated in the paper text (binding constants in nanomolar, melting temperatures in degrees Celsius, concentrations in micromolar); not a problem here.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, verified. The whole study rests on 5 DNA substrates: one native telomeric i-motif (C-NAT) and four copies of it carrying an abasic (base-missing) site at position 14, 16, 17 or 20. I counted these from the circular dichroism filenames and cross-checked against the paper text (AP14 x23, AP16 x23, AP17 x24, AP20 x21 mentions). The checklist needs about 1,500 rows, or 400 for classification.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~3.5 GB of Leica .lif microscopy stacks plus a 59 MB blot archive
a6_fits_laptop.note: The only bulky data is confocal microscopy: 16 files, several over 300 MB (one 888 MB, one 553 MB). Individually fetchable, but it is raw imaging in a vendor format and would need cell segmentation before it meant anything.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: The 5 substrate names in the circular dichroism archive match the 5 named in the paper exactly. No disagreement found - there is simply almost nothing to count.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels are genuine wet-lab measurements (gel-based cleavage assays, surface-based binding kinetics, circular dichroism melting), not another model's output. A8 is fine; the problem is quantity and packaging, not provenance.

existing_models.name: iM-Seeker (web server for predicting i-motif DNA, Nucleic Acids Research 2024)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved in detail; described as a Balanced Random Forest classifier for whether a sequence folds, plus an XGBoost (gradient-boosted trees) regressor for folding strength, trained on genome-wide antibody-based CUT&Tag sequencing data.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Not read in full; the surrounding literature frames quantitative folding stability from sequence as the open part.

existing_models.name: Prediction of DNA i-motifs via machine learning (Nucleic Acids Research 2024, 52:2188)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved; search result only. Predicts i-motif-forming sequences genome-wide.

existing_models.name: Sequence-based prioritization of i-Motif candidates in the human genome (Frontiers in Bioinformatics 2025)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not retrieved; search result reports classifiers separating i-motif-like sequences from biological and synthetic negative controls.

backbone.name: None proposed - DNA language models such as DNABERT-2 or HyenaDNA would fit the data type, but 5 sequences cannot train or even honestly evaluate a head.

integration.partner_dataset: None viable. In principle the i-motif CUT&Tag sequencing maps behind iM-Seeker could be joined on human genome coordinates, but this paper contributes 5 synthetic oligonucleotides, not genomic positions.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Cannot be written - with 5 substrates there is nothing to join.

controls.positive_control: The paper itself provides good controls (catalytically dead APE1 mutants H309N and E96A, native undamaged i-motif), but these are experimental controls, not a machine-learning positive control.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is meaningless at n=5.
controls.external_validation: None - these specific substrates were measured only here.

honest_claim_h3: No honest claim is available: with 5 measured DNA substrates any model would be fitting noise, and no held-out set can be formed.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use a short DNA sequence and where its base is missing to predict how fast a repair enzyme cuts it.
plain_idea.train_on: What I considered: one row per damaged DNA molecule, with the sequence and the position of the abasic (missing-base) site as input. Verified count available here: 5.
plain_idea.predict: How efficiently the repair enzyme APE1 cuts that molecule, and how tightly it binds. The true answer comes from gel-based cleavage assays and surface-based binding kinetics run by the authors, reported only inside figure panels.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Groups studying how DNA repair works on folded, four-stranded DNA would want a sequence-to-cleavage predictor, but it needs hundreds of substrates measured one way; this paper has 5.

more_or_better_data.why: Existing i-motif predictors (iM-Seeker, Nucleic Acids Research 2024) were trained on genome-wide antibody-based sequencing data covering many thousands of sites. This paper offers 5 synthetic oligonucleotides, verified from the circular dichroism filenames.

confidence_score.why: Triplicate measurements exist (the text says n = 3), which would in principle give a noise estimate, but 3 replicates on 5 items cannot calibrate a predictor.

models_beatable.why: The nearest existing models (2024-2025, random forest and gradient-boosted trees on genome-scale data) predict a different quantity - whether a genomic sequence folds into an i-motif - and nothing here could be used to beat them.

guaranteed_improvement.why: Fails on every condition: no shared evaluation split, a different measured quantity (enzyme cleavage versus folding status), and no join key between 5 synthetic oligonucleotides and genomic coordinates.

ml_idea: The only idea the data supports - predict APE1 cleavage efficiency from the sequence and abasic-site position of folded i-motif DNA - needs on the order of hundreds of substrates. This paper measured 5. A viable version of this project would have to assemble substrates across the APE1 literature, which is a label-construction exercise (a Part A2 failure in its own right) rather than a use of this dataset.

effort.compute_note: No estimates meaningful: the tabular working set is a 36 KB archive of spectrometer files describing 5 samples. I timed nothing because there is nothing to run.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the distinct DNA substrates. I did this in one command by unzipping the 36 KB circular dichroism archive and reading the filenames: 5 (C-NAT, AP14, AP16, AP17, AP20). That kills the project in under a minute.

verdict_reason: Fails A5 and A2, both verified in the files. The study is a careful single-topic biochemistry paper built on 5 DNA substrates (native telomeric i-motif plus abasic sites at positions 14, 16, 17 and 20), and the OSF deposit contains only proprietary instrument output - JASCO spectra, GraphPad plot files, Bio-Rad quantitative PCR runs, LI-COR blot images and ~3.5 GB of Leica confocal stacks - with no feature/label table anywhere. The 24 MB supplement is a Word document with zero tables. Measured cleavage efficiencies and binding constants exist only inside figure panels and would have to be digitised. Nothing here is modellable at any scale.
